When developing exception reports, keep in mind that the detailed data from which exception reports are derived must be available to management so that the cause of any equipment being so identified can be determined.# 6. Shop Start-Up Procedures for VMRS

As mentioned in Section 3, the key to successfully introducing VMRS into a fleet maintenance management system is the development of a logical implementation plan. This section offers guidance for logically implementing VMRS at the shop level.

Although VMRS implementation requires the cooperation of maintenance, finance, systems, and data processing departments within a company, it is still the equipment and maintenance manager's responsibility to implement VMRS at the shop level. Because the adoption of any new system can spur resistance among employees, it's important for the maintenance manager to anticipate and minimize resistance through effective planning, motivation, training, and supervision.

This section covers the following implementation topics:

- Initial Planning
- Repair Order Forms and Procedures
- Shop Personnel Training
- Shop and Central Office File Preparation
- Equipment Master Record Forms
- Procedures Manuals Development
- Follow-up Procedures

# Initial Planning for VMRS Implementation

There are two basic methods that can be used to introduce the VMRS<sup>™</sup> Repair Order and Equipment Master Record Forms into the maintenance shop. The first is to wait until the new VMRSbased management information system has been developed and tested, and perhaps even operate both old and new systems in parallel for a time. The second is to implement the forms immediately.

In the wait and see approach, Equipment Master Records are completed prior to the introduction of the repair order forms. Equipment data files are constructed and tested, but no live VMRS data is accumulated. When management is certain that the new system will work, the VMRS Repair Order Form is introduced, and data begins accumulating.

The problem with the "wait and see" approach is a major time lag is created. Several or many months may pass before meaningful data is gathered for reporting purposes. Introducing the Repair Order Form immediately is a more positive and beneficial approach.

An objective comparison of the VMRS<sup>™</sup> Repair Order Form to the fleet's existing repair order will probably show that the VMRS form can capture all of the information currently being recorded—plus a whole lot more. Prompt use of the VMRS Repair Order Form ensures data collection begins without delay, speeding implementation.

Coordination both within and outside the maintenance department should occur prior to using the Repair Order Form in the shop. Contact with the accounting and data processing departments should be made to determine their current and future information requirements. For example, there are two distinct VMRS<sup>TM</sup> Repair Order Forms—Repair Order (*Form 6*) and Special Repair Order (*Form 7*). The major difference between these forms is that the Special Repair Order form provides for the manual extension and entry of parts and labor cost. Both forms should meet fleet requirements.

As part of the planning, development, and test process for implementation of the overall system, some larger fleets have found it worthwhile to initially operate a VMRS-based system on a manual basis. Smaller fleets lacking access to computer-based systems will do this anyway.

In larger fleets, VMRS-coded data may be collected on a group of like pieces of equipment. This data is then processed manually in the format of proposed computer-generated reports. This technique offers opportunities for systems evaluation, for testing and revising reports, for gaining an actual working knowledge of the system and its potential, and for training users of the system. **Important Tip:** Make every effort to have data from the Repair Order Forms entered into the fleet maintenance management system *in the maintenance shop!* 

## **Repair Order Forms and Procedures**

The VMRS<sup>™</sup> Repair Order Form is the key to effective fleet maintenance data collection. It provides a uniform method of initiating repairs and service, and for recording pertinent information regarding these repairs. This four-part form is designed to be self-explanatory, self-coding and is intended to minimize written input by technicians. Properly completed, it offers a wealth of basic data for the equipment being reported on. Figure 6-1 illustrates the steps in the preparation of the repair order, its subsequent flow through the shop where additional data is recorded, and its completion subsequent to the equipment being returned to service. The size of the staff at each shop will determine who performs what functions. Figure 6-1 should also be viewed as an illustration of steps or functions to be performed by individuals in the preparation and completion of the repair order. If the shop has an open parts room, the technician would record the parts drawn on the repair order. The shop supervisor or a shift foreman may be responsible for inspecting the equipment, rather than an inspector. In a small shop, one individual would usually perform all of the functions shown in Figure 6-1.

The distribution and disposition of the four parts of the repair order shown in **Figure 6-1** may vary from fleet to fleet. What is both critical and essential is that:

- a. The data from the repair order be entered into the maintenance information system.
- b. In a fleet with two or more facilities, one of the first three copies of the repair order should be sent to the fleet central maintenance files to be filed in an individual equipment history jacket. (*See Shop and Central Office Files*)
- For domiciled equipment, one copy of the repair order should be filed in an equipment history jacket at the domicile location.

Individual maintenance facilities performing work on non-domiciled equipment may wish to retain on file one copy of the repair order. Temporary establishment and retention of such a file in repair order number sequence will assist in communications between the central maintenance office and local maintenance supervisors. A disposition schedule for repair order files of nondomiciled equipment should be established.

How many VMRS repair forms should you order initially? Past fleet consumption of repair orders should be used as a guide. Consumption estimates should be revised if the implementation procedures will change existing procedures under which a repair order is written. Initial procurement of repair order forms should be in a quantity sufficient to last at least three months, with a 6-12 months supply recommended as an optimum quantity.

To obtain all VMRS forms, call the Technology & Maintenance Council's customer service line at (866) 821-3468, or (703) 838-1763 outside the United States. A catalog of all VMRS-related products is available upon request.

## Training Personnel to Use the VMRS<sup>™</sup> Repair Order Form

The VMRS Repair Order Form is the first and most significant link in the fleet information management chain. Proper training in usage of this form is essential for successful implementation of VMRS.

Supervisors should be trained first. Training should be conducted by the project manager responsible for implementing VMRS. The supervisors, in turn, should train their subordinates.

Should the fleet have more than one maintenance facility, training should first be conducted at the facility closest to maintenance headquarters. Maintenance management and systems / data processing representatives should attend shop training sessions to listen to the questions and comments shop personnel will invariably offer relative to the new system. This is an invaluable source of input for system designers!

Figure 6-1

If company training on repair order forms preparation and usage is given first to supervisors, be sure upper management attends at least the first such session to motivate employees and emphasize company interest in the new system.

All VMRS participants must know the company objectives for the new system. These may include recordkeeping simplification, better record management, increased uptime, and better maintenance scheduling.

The training program must strike a balance between a need to know and a need to understand. All participants must understand the role that they play in the system. Key advantages should be pointed out, especially when time savings are gained. For example, most technicians find the use of preprinted codes to describe equipment components and labor activities significantly reduce their paperwork responsibilities.

Imaginative use of training aids such as overheads, slides, or computer-generated presentations will assist both student and instructor alike. A sample supply of forms for hands-on experience during training sessions is recommended. The step-by-step completion of these forms, by shop personnel in a training session, will add realism to the training and generate their comments and recommendations. Such sessions will also develop a great deal of information to be subsequently used in a fleet procedures manual (*See Development of Procedures Manuals*)

The following is a sample outline for the content of a shop personnel training program for supervisors, mechanics, etc., for using the VMRS<sup>™</sup> Repair Order Form.

- State objective of training session, which is to explain use of the new repair order form.
- b. State what subjects will be covered to prepare the class for the lesson.
- c. State reasons for replacing the old fleet maintenance information system with VMRS. This helps motivate the class by developing a positive attitude to deviating from established practices.
- d. Briefly describe VMRS as appropriate to

class needs. This provides a general background for shop participation in the new system.

- e. Introduce the new Repair Order form and explain the purpose of its four main parts.
- f. Explain the flow of the Repair Order through the shop. Refer to Figure 6-1 as an example of the type of handout or visual aid should be used to explain each person's role in the system.
- g. Explain the four-step process of how the Repair Order is prepared.
  - 1. Review the equipment file prior to writing the repair order.
  - Review initial write-up, heading and instructions.
  - 3. Review the mechanic's entries/copy.
  - 4. Review the part specialist's entries/ copies.
- h. Demonstrate the three-step process of how the repair order is closed.
  - Review of mechanic's copy by supervisor or inspector, certification of work/inspection, etc.
  - Completion by supervisor/clerk, transcribing data from mechanic's copy to first three copies, etc.
  - 3. Distribution of copies of completed repair order as shown in **Figure 6-1**.
- i. Provide opportunity for questions. Leave nothing unresolved. What cannot be resolved at this time must be resolved later and made known to all participants.
- Review preparation of repair orders in special situations, such as component removal and rebuilding, etc.
- k. Review practical application in repair order forms. Present sample problems to the group for role-playing exercises.
- 1. Review and summarize lesson.

A review and analysis of repair orders completed during the first week will probably show areas in which additional instruction is required at both the shop group and individual levels. A follow-up session should be held as soon as possible.

A means to provide the same instruction to new employees must be developed to ensure the continued quality of the maintenance data being collected. The development, ready availability and use of a Procedures Manual will help satisfy this requirement.

# Shop and Central Office Files

A maintenance (equipment) file folder should be established for each piece of equipment. Fleets operating more than one maintenance facility and having equipment domiciled at these different locations should establish a file for each piece of equipment at its domiciled location, as well as at the central maintenance office.

Files of domiciled equipment should be reviewed prior to writing or issuing a repair order to a mechanic. This will assist in identifying the cause of the problem (especially in instances of repeat or frequent work in the same VMRS system) rather than treatment of its symptoms. Obvious indicators of recent work on the same component for non-domiciled equipment should cause the mechanic to bring his observations to the attention of the supervisor. A request by the shop to the central maintenance office for a check of the equipment's maintenance file can then be made. The time required by this procedure to save costly but ineffective repeat work may result in significant savings over the remaining life of the equipment, or even an entire range of equipment utilizing the same component(s).

When the VMRS Equipment File is used as designed, the equipment's maintenance profile offers ready indicators of repeat work. File personnel can be taught to identify these indicators and bring them to the attention of technically qualified persons for further evaluation and appropriate action.

# **Equipment Master Record Forms**

Equipment identification data should enter the equipment and maintenance recordkeeping system once, at its source! This data should then be distributed, or made available to all departments requiring them in whole or in part. The VMRS Equipment Master Record Form provides the means of recording essential equipment identification data. Detailed instructions for the preparation of these forms are found elsewhere in this *Handbook*.

Equipment Master Record preparation may require data input from one or more departments. Equipment characteristics and component data may be provided by the equipment and maintenance department, financial data by the accounting department, and work assignment, location, and licensing data by the operations department. Responsibility for preparing master records should be assigned to one department which will obtain all necessary data companywide.

Copies of Equipment Master Records should be filed in individual equipment file folders. Fax additional copies when required. Financial data need not be recorded on copies of master records maintained in maintenance facility equipment files which are accessible to all personnel. All but financial data can be entered on the copy of the master record in the central equipment file after entry.

Preparing Equipment Master Record forms can normally best be accomplished by maintenance facility administrative personnel. These individuals are well suited for this task because of their general knowledge of the fleet's equipment, and descriptive terminology used. Maintenance personnel are generally better equipped to obtain the data needed to properly complete master records. Sources of equipment identification data are lineset tickets, specification sheets, licensing and registration records. As a last resort, physical inspection of the equipment may be needed to produce necessary data. The value of time spent collecting data on equipment that will be traded within 12-18 months should be considered. Skeletonized records may suffice in such cases. What is important is that all equipment be entered in the total fleet inventory and that all new equipment entering the fleet have a master record prepared prior to service entry.

Detail to be entered on Equipment Master Record forms is a subjective choice for each fleet. Because record preparation usually occurs only once while the equipment is in fleet service, the value of complete versus partial data should be weighed. Completed master records can be the source of virtually unlimited maintenance data and information. Conversely, partially completed master records are ultimately a limiting factor to a fleet. Experience has shown that as users become more experienced in VMRS, they demand more information from it than was initially envisioned.

The VMRS Equipment Master Record may also be used for both developing and listing new equipment and component specifications to aid in soliciting uniform bids from equipment manufacturers.

# **Developing a Procedures Manual**

Procedure manuals document how a system works and what roles each participant plays in its operation. The manual's purpose is to ensure standardization necessary for effectively implementing system goals. Non-standardized preparation of repair order forms will cause problems in data entry and report preparation. Under these conditions, the value of the maintenance information produced suffers and company assets are wasted.

Good procedure manuals are not set in concrete, however. Consider them dynamic references which can be changed, when necessary, by the issuing authority. A loose-leaf ringed-binder format is recommended.

Procedure manuals are only useful if used. They must be made available to the user and prepared in legible formats that will encourage their use. Their arrangement should suit the user's needs, not the author's literary preferences.

A table of contents and index should be included to assist the user's ability to access the information. Index tab dividers are a good means of separating the manual into logical groups of related material. Procedure manuals should contain flowcharts, diagrams, documents and any other illustrations that will assist users in understanding specific procedures.

Descriptions of individual data entry procedures on forms should follow the arrangement of the form and the progressive sequence in which the data is to be entered. Use of sample forms annotated with sequential procedure numbers keyed to written instructions is recommended. Copies of completed forms should also be included when appropriate. Each procedure described should begin on a new page. The purpose and/or objective of the procedure should be simply stated in a single sentence at the beginning of the procedure being described. If the overall procedure began prior to the application of the specific procedure at hand, the previous procedure should be identified. Subsequently, when the specific procedure is completed, the concluding sentence should either describe who does what or state that the overall procedure is now complete.

Users of procedure manuals are an invaluable source for manual improvement. Encourage user input. Test suggestions in a controlled setting, and implement if effective.

Management should routinely spot check procedure manuals to ensure changes have been entered correctly, outdated material has been discarded, and that persons using the manual are aware of any changes made.

# Follow-up Procedures

Training programs and procedure manuals alone do not guarantee that data input will be of an acceptable quality. Follow-up procedures are a must for ensuring data quality.

Supervision is one follow-up method of maintaining data input quality. Repair order forms must be checked by supervisors when completed by mechanics and parts specialists. Errors must be corrected immediately.

Supervisors have two choices: They can correct the errors and eventually become edit clerks, or they can have the appropriate individuals correct the entries and thereby remain functional supervisors.

Periodic spot checking or auditing of repair order forms is a good idea. Errors noted should be promptly brought to the attention of supervisors for further correction. This can be troublesome if the maintenance facility in question is distant from the maintenance manger's central office. In these cases, well-developed and documented procedures — reinforced by supervision, auditing, and data editing routines — will help minimize problems. People are generally happier and more productive when they have some understanding of their role in the organization, what they are doing, and can have their questions answered. Contact with subordinates, and auditing, will help achieve accurate implementation of VMRS at all levels.

# 7. How to Prepare VMRS<sup>™</sup> Forms

There are five basic forms in the VMRS system:

- Equipment Master Record—Power Units (Form 1)
- Equipment Master Record—Trailers (Form 2)
- VMRS Equipment File (Form 30)
- Repair Order Form (*Form 6*)
- Special Repair Order Form (*Form* 7)

Three additional forms allow the recording of additional data on equipment components beyond that allowed by the basic forms:

- Mechanical Refrigeration Master Record (*Form 3*)
- Equipment Master Record -Material Handling (*Form 4*)
- Equipment Master Record Continuation Form (*Form* 25)

These forms available in hard-copy format; however, the data elements contained therein could easily be applied to electronic forms within a in-house or third-party provided fleet maangement system.

# Instructions for Completing Equipment Master Records

# Equipment Master Record – Power Units (Form 1)

The following instructions have been designed to serve as a logical guide for completing the VMRS "Equipment Master Record—Power Units" form. Field experience has shown that this essentially "one time task" can be accurately accomplished by clerical personnel with minimal training based on these instructions.

The Equipment Master Record—Power Units form or *"Form 1"* provides a detailed descriptive record of a piece of equipment and its major components. It provides for the recording of data which can be used by management responsible for the financial, licensing, operations and safety functions, in addition to engineering and maintenance aspects of fleet operations.

Proper preparation of all VMRS forms is vital to ensuring useful data, and minimizing errors and redundancy. Completing the entire form — even though it may seem to serve no clear purpose initially — will save much labor and effort later when the fleet's maintenance information system is more fully used.

## Data Entry

Each field of data on the Equipment Master Record (EMR) *Form 1* is assigned a number, and beyond the basic heading information, each line on the form is assigned a letter. Thus, the data code for the main transmission would be entered on Line "H," Block "7" under the caption "TRANS TYPE CODE — MAIN 7."

**Figure 7-1** (page 133) is a blank example of EMR *Form 1*. **Figure 7-2** shows a completed EMR *Form 1*. **Figure 7-3** shows an example of the EMR Continuation form or *"Form 25,"* which is used as a supplement to EMR *Form 1*.

The following guidelines will describe each title, line, and block number; its corresponding instruction; and the source where the requested information may be obtained. A single asterisk (\*) in the left hand margin identifies minimum data required for original entry of the equipment into a fleet's database (Program Control A). A double asterisk (\*\*) identifies items that should be recorded when changing previously submitted equipment data. (Program Control E).

Additionally, quick reference tables are provided in this section for assignment of the most common equipment, engine, transmission and rear axle "Type Codes." Diagrams are also provided which further illustrate the type code structures. These diagrams should be helpful for assigning type codes that are not obtainable from the basic reference tables provided. # Instructions for Completing Equipment Master Records

Master Record Continuation Form – (Form 25)

The following instructions are provided for those equipment users who wish to record optional data on components beyond those provided for on the basic Equipment Master Record —Power Units (*Form 1*). Equipment users who elect to record such additional data are still urged to use all appropriate VMRS Code Keys when completing *Form 25* as is done when completing *Form 1*.

| Title/Line/Block No.                | Instruction                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Source                  |
|-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------|
| 1. Blocks 1-8                       | Complete Blocks 1-8 as per instructions for <i>Form 1</i> .                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | See Form 1 instructions |
| 2. Make (Position 1)                | Enter manufacturer/supplier/brand five character alpha code.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Code Key 34             |
| 3. Model (Position 2)               | Enter manufacturer's model number.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Manufacturer            |
| 4. Serial (Position 3)              | Enter exactly as shown.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Manufacturer            |
| 5. Description Type<br>(Position 4) | Enter (optional) description of system, assembly or part in 11 characters or less.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Company                 |
| 6. System (Position 5)              | Enter three-digit system code.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Code Key 31             |
| 7. Assembly (Position 6)            | Enter three-digit assembly code.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | Code Key 32             |
| 8. Component (Position 7)           | Enter three-digit component code.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Code Key 33             |
| 9. Sequence (Position 8)            | The sequence number establishes the order of entry for "Other Equipment" coded on designated likes of Master Record forms for data processing purposes. Enter "10" for the first item of other equipment recorded. For second and subsequent items entered, increase the basic Sequence Number by 10, so that the sequence appears "10," "20," 30," and so on. If the description of the component being coded (Position 4) requires more than 11 characters, continue the description on the next line using using the same field to reenter the system/assembly/component code from the preceding line, and increase the number by "1" for each additional line needed. Thus, a single component requiring three lines to describe might have Sequence Numbers 40, 41, 42. |                         |

## Instructions for Completing Equipment Master Records Mechanical Refrigeration Master Record — (Form 3)

This form records information for mechanical refrigeration units designed to operate on trucks, trailers, or containers. It is designed to provide a detailed descriptive record of individual mechanical refrigeration units and their major components. **Figure 7-6** illustrates a completed form. The EMR Master Record Continuation form (*Form 25*) may be used to record additional data whenever necessary for maintenance information purposes.

Asterisks (\*) in the margins of the following pages identify suggested minimum data required for original entry of individual units into each fleet's equipment data base (Program Control R). Double asterisks (\*\*) identify items that should be recorded when changing previously submitted data (Program Control T). Complete all blocks whenever possible.

All of the forms described in this section may be obtained by contacting The Technology & Maintenance Council's VMRS Customer Service Department at: TMC's VMRS Customer Service, 950 N. Glebe Road, Arlington, VA 22203. Phone: (866) 821-3468 ; (703) 838-1763.

# Instructions for Completing Equipment Master Record – Material Handling – Form 4

This form records information for material handling equipment designed to operate on various types of equipment. It is designed to provide a detailed descriptive record of individual mechanical refrigeration units and their major components. **Figure 7-7** illustrates a completed form. The EMR Master Record Continuation form (*Form 25*) may be used to record additional data whenever necessary for maintenance information purposes.

Asterisks (\*) in the margins of the following pages identify suggested minimum data required for original entry of individual units into each fleet's equipment data base (Program Control M). Double asterisks (\*\*) identify items that should be recorded when changing previously submitted data (Program Control P). Complete all blocks whenever possible.

All of the forms described in this section may be obtained by contacting The Technology & Maintenance Council's VMRS Customer Service Department at: TMC VMRS Customer Service, 2200 Mill Road, Alexandria, VA 22314. Phone: (800) ATA-LINE ; (703) 838-1754

# Instructions for Completing Equipment Master Records

# Equipment Master Record—Trailers, Containers, Converters (Form 2)

The following instructions have been designed to serve as a logical guide for completing the VMRS "Equipment Master Record—Trailers, Containers, Converters" form.

*"Form 2"* provides a detailed descriptive record of the equipment and its major components. It provides for the recording of data which can be used by management responsible for the financial, licensing, operations and safety functions, in addition to engineering and maintenance aspects of fleet operations.

Proper preparation of all VMRS forms is vital to ensuring useful data, and minimizing errors and redundancy. Completing the entire form — even though it may seem to serve no clear purpose initially — will save much labor and effort later when the fleet's maintenance information system is more fully used.

The following guidelines will describe each title, line and block number; its corresponding instruction; and the source where the requested information may be obtained.

A single asterisk (\*) in the left hand margin identifies minimum data required for original entry of the equipment into a fleet's equipment database (Program Control C). A double asterisk (\*\*) identifies items that should be recorded when changing previously submitted equipment data (Program Control F).

Additionally, quick reference tables are provided in this section for assignment of the most common equipment, engine, transmission and rear axle Type Codes. Diagrams are also provided which further illustrate the Type Code structures. These diagrams should be helpful for assigning type codes that are not obtainable from the basic reference tables provided.

All of the forms described in this section may be obtained by contacting The Technology & Maintenance Council's VMRS Customer Service Department at:

> TMC / ATA VMRS Customer Service 950 N. Glebe Road Arlington, VA 22203 Phone: (866) 821-3468 Phone: (703) 838-1763

# Instructions for Completing VMRS<sup>™</sup> Repair Orders

There are two types of repair orders used with VMRS<sup>TM</sup>:

- The Repair Order (Form 6) and
- The Special Repair Order (*Form 7*)

*Form 6* is primarily intended for fleets which:

- have access to data processing equipment.
- intend to use the equipment to make parts and labor cost calculations for maintenance reporting and accounting purposes.
- perform most maintenance "in-house."

The *Form* 7 is primarily intended for fleets which use manual record keeping systems and for use as a purchase order/repair order record for maintenance and repair services purchased from vendors (out-sourced maintenance).

Both forms serve three basic purposes:

- Provide a document for recording maintenance history data. Coding to the three-digit system level (code key 31) will provide sufficient parts cost information for this purpose.
- Provide a means of recording detailed parts history data for inventory control purposes. Coding at the nine-digit component level (code key 33) is required for this purpose.
- 3. Provide a basic visual record for both shop and statutory purposes in conjunction with the VMRS Equipment File.

# VMRS Repair Order (Form 6) Instructions

The Repair Order (*Form 6*) is a four-part document set consisting of:

- Data processing copy (original)
- Equipment History Jacket (copy)
- Facility File or Vendor Copy (copy)
- Mechanic's Copy (copy)

The following instructions cover preparation of the data processing and mechanic's copies. Instructions preceded by the word "optional" are included for those wishing to compile component code data (code key 33) beyond the system level of detail (code key 31).

Asterisks (\*) identify data recommended for input into maintenance information databases.

Coding maintenance data or auxiliary engines may be accomplished by using Code Keys 31-33 as appropriate. This will preclude entry of erroneous data into maintenance databases. When necessary to record maintenance data at the component level for auxiliary engines, appropriate power codes may be used provided that separate equipment master records have been created for such equipment.

The back of the Repair Order contains a list of system codes (code key 31) and descriptions for easy reference.

All of the forms described in this section may be obtained by contacting The Technology & Maintenance Council's VMRS Customer Service Department at:

The Repair Order Form may also be used in recording outside repairs. However, the Special Repair Order Form (*Form 7*) is better suited for this purpose.

# Special Instructions for Completing the Repair Order Form (Form 6)

#### (When Used to Record Towing Activity)

Repair Order forms may be used to assign personnel and equipment to perform towing. This enables data collection for properly identifying towing expense to each piece of equipment so moved by an equipment operator.

Towing may be accomplished by companyowned or vendor-owned equipment under the following conditions:

- From one company site to another
- From field to company site
- From field to vendor site
- From vendor to company site

If company owned equipment was used, the Work Accomplished code (Code Key 15) would be "20 - Towing" and the Repair Site code (Code Key 17) would be "1 - Facility." The appropriate "Reason for Repair" (Code Key 14) and "Repair Class" (Code Key 16) would also be checked.

When completing the Repair Order when vendor owned equipment was used, the Work Accomplished Code (Code Key 15) would be "20 - Towing," and the Repair Site code (code key 17) would be "4 - Outside Company." Again, the appropriate "Reason for Repair" (Code Key 14) and "Repair Class" (Code Key 16) would be checked.

It is not necessary to enter specific systems data in the Labor Information portion of the Repair Order prepared for towing.

Upon completion of the towing, the related Repair Order form is completed. A subsequent repair order is then prepared to accomplish required repairs or maintenance to the equipment.

# Special Instructions for Completing the Repair Order Form (Form 6)

#### (When Used to Record Diagnostics, Inspections, Painting, and Retrofit)

Repair Order forms may be used to assign work to be performed on equipment without data for specific component codes being recorded for labor or parts, hours, issues, and costs. In addition to towing, other situations arise in which work is performed on the entire piece of equipment. Diagnostic checks, inspection of equipment for statutory purposes, painting equipment, etc., are examples of this. In addition, government regulations may require modifications to be made to currently-owned equipment.

Identity of maintenance items such as these will enable proper identification of cost data essential for individual justification of fleet maintenance and equipment budgets and expenses. Such data may also be valuable for company and industry justification of rate increases, commentary on effects of equipment regulation, etc.

#### 1. Inspections

When inspection of the entire piece of equipment occurs, one of each of the following codes will be assigned when preparing the Repair Order form.

- Reason for Repair (code key 14)
- Repair Class (code key 16)
- Repair Site (code key 17)
- Work Accomplished (code key 15)

The Reason for Repair Code could be:

- Inspection, Routine-05
- Special Study—24
- Statutory Inspection—34

The Repair Class Code could be:

- Scheduled—1
- Nonscheduled—2
- Emergency—3

The Repair Site Code could be:

- Facility—1
- Field—2
- Terminal—3
- Outside Company—4

The Work Accomplished Code is 06 for inspect.

#### 2. Diagnostics

The development of sophisticated equipment diagnostics has created a situation where the diagnostic function is often separate from the on-vehicle work performed by a mechanic. As always, the key to obtaining or retrieving diagnostic information is the proper coding of data at the source, at the time the action took place.

In the case of a diagnostic check, the Reason for Repair (code key 14) may logically be the result of any of the following:

- 01 Breakdown
- 02 Consumption, Fuel
- 03 Consumption, Oil
- 04 Driver's Report
- 05 Inspection, Routine
- 07 Pre-delivery
- 08 PM
- 09 Rework

#### 3. Equipment Retrofit

#### (Statutory Modification)

Reason for Repair Code "35—Statutory Modification" will highlight equipment expense prompted by government-mandated retrofits.

#### 4. Painting a Portion of the Equipment

When a portion of a piece of equipment is painted as part of a specific repair, systems codes are recorded for the labor associated with the painting. Examples are painting:

- as part of body work.
- of a major component following overhaul.
- a portion of the equipment following some modification or part installation.

Appropriate Reason for Repair Codes (code key 14) include:

- 09 Rework
- 11 Routine Maintenance
- 22 Conversion
- 24 Special Study
- 31/32 Accidents
- 35 Statutory Modification
- 37 Vandalism
- 38 Warranty

#### 5. Painting the Entire Piece of Equipment.

When an entire piece of equipment is painted, and the work performed is not the result of a repair action that required painting to complete, one of each of the following codes should be entered on the Repair Order form:

Reason For Repair (code key 14)

- 11 Routine
- 21 Capital Improvement
- 22 Conversion
- 23 Modification
- 24 Special Study
- 34 Statutory Modification
- 38 Warranty

Repair Class (code key 16)

- 1 Scheduled
- 2 Nonscheduled
- 3 Emergency

Repair Site (code key 17)

- 1 Facility
- 2 Field
- 3 Terminal
- 4 Outside Company

Work Accomplished (code key 15)

13 Other Maintenance or Repair

The Work Accomplished Code "13" is applicable for all seven Reasons for Repair listed above. The indication that work accomplished applies to the entire piece of equipmeng is the reason for omitting any systems data under labor information.

#### Special Instructions for Completing the Repair Order Form (Form 6) For Completing Warranty Work

Properly prepared Repair Order forms are an excellent data source for the support and documentation of warranty claims and for the development of warranty information systems files.

When known warranty work is to be performed on a piece of equipment, a repair order should be prepared with the Reason for Repair (code key 14) "38, Warranty." No other work should be performed on the equipment and recorded the repair order. This requirement allows easy identification of warranty data within a maintenance information system.

The mechanic should perform the prescribed work on the piece of equipment and complete

the Mechanic's Copy as described previously. It may be necessary to assist the parts specialist in identifying and coding specific data in the their completion of the parts information portion of the repair order.

The parts specialist will issue the necessary parts and enter the appropriate parts data in accordance with Repair Order form Instructions 29-35. In entering the parts data it is essential that only the part failure code for the specific part that failed under warranty be entered. No parts failure code should be entered for additional parts which had to be replaced as a result of the failed part.

If, in the course of work, a potential warranty situation is identified, a separate Repair Order form should be prepared and the required warranty repair performed under this repair order as outline previously. Similarly, if in the process of reviewing the repair order, the supervisor or inspector notes work should be categorized as "38, Warranty," a new repair order should be prepared for such work under the warranty classification. The applicable parts, parts failure, and labor data should be deleted from all copies of the first Repair Order form and transferred to the new "Warranty" Repair Order form.

NOTE: In the development and functioning of maintenance management information systems which identify warranty data, it is essential that in the subsequent settlement of warranty claims the fact of the claim not be eliminated. Full or partial cost figures may be adjusted, but complete removal of the claim identity will distort future evaluations and comparisons of pieces of equipment, their specifications, components and manufacturer performance in claims adjustments.

#### Instructions for Completing the Special Repair Order Form (Form 7)

The Special Repair Order form is a four-part form, similar to the Repair Order form (*Form* 6), but intended for use with manual record keeping systems or for recording out-sourced maintenance activity.

Instructions for completing *Form* 7 follow. Asterisks(\*) identify data recommended for input into maintenance information databases.

#### STEP 1

The Shop Supervisor or other person assigned the responsibility for the initial preparation of the Special Repair Order form completes Instructions 1-17 as detailed previously for the Repair Order form. Additionally, in the case of outside repairs, the Shop Supervisor enters the vendor's identity in the block provided (i.e., vendor). The vendor will, in turn, assign and enter the invoice number in the block provided.

#### STEP 2

The Mechanic enters data on the Mechanic's Copy of the Special Repair Order form in accordance with Instructions 18-28 as detailed previously for the Repair Order form.

#### STEP 3

The Parts Specialist enters data on the Special Repair Order form in accordance with Instructions 29-35 as detailed previously for the Repair Order form, and as follows:

#### Instruction 34.1

Upon completion of "34—Unit Price," multiply "QTY" times "Unit Price" and enter result in the "Parts Cost" column.

#### Instruction 34.2

Total the "Parts Cost" column, apply parts tax as applicable and enter the Total Parts Cost figure in the block provided.

#### Instruction 34.3 Transfer the Total Parts Cost from 34.2 to the field "Enter Total Parts Cost Here".

#### STEP 4

The Inspector completes the entries on the Special Repair Order as previously detailed in Instructions 36 and 37 of the Repair Order form.

#### STEP 5

The Shop Clerk enters data on the Special Repair Order and the Mechanic's Copy as previously detailed in Instructions 39-45 of the Repair Order form, and as follows:

#### Instruction 44.1

Upon completion of Instruction 44, "Actual Time," multiply "Actual Time" times the established labor rate and enter result in the "Labor Cost" column.

#### Instruction 44.2\*

Total the "Actual Time," "Labor Cost," and "Standard Time" (optional) columns and enter totals in the appropriate blocks provided.

#### Instruction 44.3\*

Enter "Total Parts Cost" in the block provided, if not already done from 34.3.

#### Instruction 44.4\*

Total the "Labor" and "Parts Cost" and enter the amount in the field marked "Enter Total Amount Due Here."

#### STEP 6

The Shop Supervisor completes his entries and reviews the Special Repair Order form in accordance with Instructions 47-49 as previously detailed for the Repair Order form.

#### Instructions for Completing the Special Repair Order Form (Form 7) as a Purchase Order for Outside Services

The design of the Special Repair Order (*Form 7*) enhances its ability to serve as combination purchase order/repair record for maintenance and repair services obtained from vendors. Fleets with in-house data processing services which use the Repair Order form (*Form 6*) may find the Special Repair Order (*Form 7*) is better suited to document vendor-provided services.

The following instructions provide detailed guidance for recording vendor maintenance services data. It is recognized that the relationship between any given fleet and its individual vendors will probably vary. It is also recognized that vendors do, in varying degrees, have the ability to provide the data needed to support the maintenance management information requirements of the fleet customers. Therefore, it is not unreasonable for a fleet to expect the support of its vendors, with regard to providing data in certain specified formats, in the highly competitive market of fleet services.

Examples of out-sourced maintenance activities that would be appropriate uses of the Special Repair Order form include equipment maintenance, component rebuilding, and road calls.

#### **Preparing the Special Repair Order for Vendor Services**

#### A. Fleet Actions

1. Prepare the heading of the Special Repair Order by entering the following information:

- company and facility code
- facility identification
- date
- meter reading
- equipment ID number
- company name
- activity code

#### 2. Check the appropriate code for:

- Reason for Repair
- Repair Priority (check only one)
- Repair Site (check 4, Outside Company)
- Continuation Repair Order

3. Under "Date Promised," enter the date/time the vendor estimates the work will be completed. If unknown, leave blank.

4. Enter the name of the person authorizing the work to be performed/services provided under "Written By."

5. Under "Instructions," describe the work and/ or services to be performed.

6. Enter the name of the vendor who has agreed to perform the work or services on the equipment in the box "Vendor Notification."

7. If parts are provided by the fleet, enter the appropriate VMRS codes, manufacturers parts

numbers, and quantities provided in the "Parts Information" (left) side of the Special Repair Order. Complete pricing as outlined in Instruction 21 below. For each part used in preventive maintenance routines, enter "PM" in the Condition Code Column.

8. Detach the Data Processing (first) copy from the Special Repair Order form to the vendor.

B. Vendor Actions

For the fleet to gain the potential benefits from using the Special Repair Order for outside maintenance, the vendor must understand why the form is important. When a continuing relationship exists between the fleet and the vendor, obtaining the cooperation of the vendor and vendor's mechanics in properly completing this largely self-coding form should present no serious obstacle. It will be far more productive for both fleet and vendor alike if the vendor and its mechanics and parts specialists enter the required data in accordance with the information provided on the front and back of the mechanic's copy of the form.

10. Perform repairs/services as specified under "Instructions." Instructions 11-19 describe the steps to be taken by the vendor in completion of the Special Repair Order form.

11. For every chargeable part, the vendor enters under:

- "Part Number," the manufacturer's part number.
- "Quantity," the quantity used
- "Unit Price," the cost of each item, pair set, kit, etc.
- "Parts Cost," the cost per unit (Quantity x Unit Price)
- For parts used in preventive maintenance routines, enter "PM" in the Condition Code Column.

Refer to the back of the mechanic's copy of the Special Repair Order Form. For each part issued, determine and then enter the appropriate threedigit system code under the "SYS." column in the "Parts Information" section of the form.

Compute and enter parts tax in the appropriate box. Total the "Parts Cost" column and enter in the appropriate box. 12. Parts failure data may be recorded by either the vendor or fleet in the Condition Code Column. See Instruction 22 below. Parts failure codes are listed on the back of the mechanic's copy of the repair order. Enter parts failure codes (optional).

13. "Labor Information" is entered on the mechanic's copy of the Special Repair Order by the vendor for, or by, each and every mechanic whose labor is charged, as follows:

- Employee number or name
- Each equipment system repaired by system/assembly code
- The appropriate "Work Accomplished Code" (from the list provided on the face of the mechanic's copy of the repair order) in the "Work Accomplished" column.
- The time spent working on this system in hours and minutes in the "Elapsed Time" column.
- Repeat process described in Instruction 12 for each equipment system serviced.

14. Transcribe the foregoing labor data from the mechanic's copy of the repair order to the appropriate "Labor Information" columns on the first two copies of the repair order. Under the column "Actual Time," convert and enter in hours and tenths of hours, the corresponding time each mechanic recorded by system.

15. Enter the labor cost per equipment system, per mechanic, in the column marked "Labor Cost" on the first two copies of the repair order.

16. Where a standard or flat rate schedule exists, enter the "Standard Time" for each corresponding task performed.

17. Total the actual time, labor cost and standard time in the corresponding columns and enter.

18. Enter the "Total Parts Cost" in the appropriate box.

19. Total labor and parts costs and enter in the "Total Amount Due" box.

20. Prepare and invoice. Enter the invoice number in the appropriate box on the Special Repair Order form. Enter the Special Repair Order form number on the invoice form. 21. Return the Equipment File Copy of the Special Repair Order and invoice (or a copy thereof) to the fleet with the piece of equipment.

#### C. Fleet Actions

22. Inspect the equipment to ensure that the repairs/services requested were properly performed and that the equipment is in a safe operating condition. The equipment inspector signs "Inspected By" and enter "Date Inspected" in appropriate boxes on the form.

23. Match the fleet file (data processing) copy of the Special Repair Order form to the copy returned by the vendor. If parts were provided by the fleet, enter and extend the parts cost and total the parts column on both copies of the repair order. 24. Review the vendor-returned copy of the repair order for data accuracy. Edit as needed. Transcribe the necessary detail from the vendor-returned copy to the data processing copy of the repair order. Enter parts failure codes (optional).

25. File the Equipment File Copy of the Special Repair Order form in the Equipment file folder.

26. Forward the data processing copy of the repair order in accordance with company procedures.

27. Process the vendor's invoice for payment inaccordance with company procedures.

# Instructions for Completing The VMRS Equipment File (*Form 30*)

#### Introduction

The VMRS<sup>™</sup> Equipment File (*Form 30*) satisfies two basic requirements for efficient fleet management.

- It provides a simple and effective means of ensuring compliance with Section 396.2 of the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Regulations.
- It enhances both daily and long-term fleet maintenance operations and record keeping requirements by providing:
  - a descriptive ready reference of each unit, its major components and service function within the fleet.
  - a visual record of the maintenance history of the unit.
  - a means of filing, in a single location and safeguarding, all pertinent records of the unit required by both regulatory agencies, as well as the demands of effective fleet management.

A VMRS Equipment File should be established for each major unit of fleet equipment at the time of acquisition or entry into service. Furthermore, no maintenance service— or repair order — should begin on a piece of equipment until the shop foreman checks the equipment's history. Equipment files should be readily accessible to persons responsible for preparing repair orders for this very purpose.

In cases where multiple maintenance facilities require centralized record keeping, these files provide a ready means for semi-skilled persons to initially identify repetitive work on the same equipment system. In such cases, the complete file being brought to the prompt attention of technically qualified persons may result in significant financial savings.

While designed for use in conjunction with VMRS, the VMRS Equipment File has proven itself to be highly effective in its use by fleets which have not yet implemented VMRS.

### Establishing VMRS Equipment Files

#### 1. General

Enter that information which best suits the nature of your operation and the requirements of Section 396.2 of the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations.

NOTE: The VMRS Equipment File is designed for records of power units—mainly trucks and tractors. However, it may also be effectively used for keeping records on other powered and non-powered pieces of equipment.

Use of this file will enable all levels of management to have a quick, visible profile of the maintenance service record of each unit maintained. It is not intended that this file replace the detailed maintenance information obtainable from maintenance information systems. This file is principally for shop level use with domiciled equipment. It may also be of value in central maintenance file systems.

The contents of this File should contain the following items:

- Equipment Master Record, line set tickets, "Spec" sheets, or similar documents which identify or describe the equipment and its components.
- All repair orders written (maintenance and mechanic's copy), including records of lubrication and inspection.
- All vendor invoices received (originals or copies).
- All driver reports received (originals or copies).
- All Tire Records maintained.

#### 2. Preparation and Use

A. Enter required information on front and inside back covers.

- Unless a significant difference exists, the "Acquired" date and the date-in-service of the unit should be considered the same.
- "Assignment" and "Location" should be kept current. Changes in status from Linehaul to P&D, etc., should be made whenever occurring.
- Enter "Beginning" miles or hours as of the date the equipment was acquired. Do not record meter readings in tenths.
- Enter appropriate detail for major compo-

nents in the space provided. Entries in the "Beginning" column should be updated when components are changed. This will provide a source of life-to-date information.

B. Entries reflecting service performed should be at time the repair order is filed.

- Use one line for each repair order (or repair order line if desired), entering repair order date, R. O. number, and meter reading (hours or miles) in the columns provided, then insert the repair order in the Equipment File folder.
- Enter record of PMs, lubrications, or inspections in the PM column in accordance with the appropriate Work Accomplished code (code key 15).
- Enter the appropriate Work Accomplished code (code key 15) in the column beneath the system on which work was preformed. Alternatively, if the Work Accomplished code is not known or used at all simply enter an "X" in the column and/or the total dollars expended on each system for parts and labor to provide a basic equipment maintenance cost record. If a pre-headed column is not provided for the system worked on, use the "Other" column.
- The "Remarks or Total Dollars" column is intended for brief explanations and notes. If cost figures are posted the total dollars from the repair order may be entered in this column.

C. As work is done continue entering maintenance service records on outside back of the Equipment File and then inside the front flap. Insert continuation sheets (VMRS *Form 31*) as needed.

# Instructions for Completing The VMRS Repair Order Log (*Form 20/21*)

#### Introduction

The VMRS<sup>™</sup> Repair Order Log (Form 20) provides fleet management with a way to help control and measure performance within its maintenance shop operations. It provides maintenance supervisors with a simple, consolidated record of repair orders written and their status (i.e., open, completed, work delayed, etc.). The second copy of the log may be used as an analysis tool of shop operations and as a data entry form for maintenance management information systems. The subsequent processing of this data can provide management with meaningful information as described further in this section. With this information at hand, supervisors can better maintain control of the assignment of the work force and the allocation of the available work space.

The one-part VMRS Repair Order Log (*Form 21*) can be used in the maintenance shop to assist shop foremen and shift supervisors in scheduling work priority, ensuring continuity of work from shift-to-shift, responding to inquires as to the availability of equipment, and aiding in monitoring the status of work in progress. When delays occur, they should be entered in the log so that corrective action can be taken, responsible managers notified, and scheduling adjustments made to keep the maintenance facility operating efficiently.

Data contained in properly completed Repair Order Logs include:

- Identity of maintenance facility.
- Period covered.
- Equipment type and ID number.
- Repair Order Number.
- Reason for Repair (code key 14).
- Repair Class (code key 16).
- Repair Site (code key 17).
- Date and hour the equipment was received by the maintenance department.
- Date and hour the maintenance department scheduled the return of the equipment to service.
- Primary reason for any delays in meeting scheduled "return to service" time.
- Actual date and hour the equipment is

returned to service.

• Any other essential information, which may be included in the "Remarks" column of the Repair Order Log.

Fleet management must determine what uses are to be made from the data contained in the Repair Order Log and whether the one- or twopart Repair Order Log is best suited for their purposes. If the Repair Order Log data is used in preparing management reports, reporting periods must be established and the appropriate entries made in the "Begin" and "End" data blocks located in the heading of each Repair Order Log sheet.

The following instructions show how to complete the VMRS Repair Order Log (*form 20/21*). An asterisk (\*) identifies data recommended for fleet database input.

#### Using the Repair Order Log

Data obtained from the Repair Order Log and other maintenance data sources should be an integral part of any fleet maintenance management information system.

The primary purpose of analyzing data from shop logs is to identify shop locations having difficulty completing their jobs on schedule. It can also aid in determining the causes of time overruns so appropriate corrective actions can be taken. Bear in mind, schedule completion times may be unrealistic due to pressures from outside the shop or of ineffective estimating techniques. An appropriate management level should consider evidence that such problems exist and take steps to speed improvements.

If the scheduled out times are realistic, failure analysis will highlight problems which interfere with shop and equipment operations productivity. Investments in increased parts inventory, or additional mechanics, space, or tools may be justifiable. If the resources are available, supervision and management functions may need improvement. This section provides several samples of reports which can be developed from Repair Order Logs.

**Report 7-1**, "Analysis of Maintenance Scheduling/Performance" identifies and compares the validity of shop scheduling forecasts vs. shop performance. The value of the report is increased when job standards are used in the shop work scheduling process. Because of shop organization and equipment types, it may be advisable to prepare this report in several categories, such as "Power Units—Linehaul."

**Report 7-2**, "Reasons for Delay, By Facility" identifies the causes of work not being completed within acceptable norms or established standards. Management must determine corrective measures (i.e., distributing work better between under-used and overworked shops).

**Report 7-3**, "Reason for Delay, By Facility, and Shift, Power Units" identifies the causes of work not being completed within acceptable norms or established standards. This report provides detail not contained in Report 7-2 and is especially useful in multi-shift shop operations.

#### Summary

The VMRS Repair Order Log assists in organizing work at hand and/or anticipated work. When used in a multi-shift operation, the Log enables each oncoming shift supervisor to quickly gain an understanding of the continuing as well as incoming work load. This permits the orderly assignment of work based on known priorities and available labor.

The Repair Order Log, like the Repair Order form, is a valuable source of data for the development of maintenance management information reports. For these purposes, the two-part Repair Order Log (*Form 20*) should be used.

The sample reports shown in this section are for illustrative purposes only. Each fleet maintenance organization should analyze its information requirements and design its own reports accordingly.

## Appendix: The Complete VMRS<sup>™</sup> Coding Convention — Code Keys 1- 84

The heart of VMRS<sup>™</sup> is the VMRS coding convention. This coding convention is divided into separate and distinct data sets called "Code Keys." Within each individual "Code Key," are individual values that identify and classify various aspects of maintenance, equipment, and maintenance management.

Individuals often mistakenly think VMRS is just the nine digit code that identifies parts. In reality, this "component" code — which comes from VMRS Code Key 33 — is only one aspect of VMRS. There are many other Code Keys within the VMRS coding convention.

Code Keys 1-13 and 34-51 identify and classify vehicle characteristics, function and specifications. Because these Code Keys are used in completing the VMRS Equipment Master Record, they are often referred to as the "Equipment Master Record codes."

The codes within Code Key 1 describe equipment vocation (i.e., linehaul, utility, etc.). Code Keys 2-13 describe equipment category and type. Code Key 20 describes equipment status/ availability for service.

Code Key 34 identifies equipment manufacturers, suppliers and brands using a five-character alpha code developed exclusively for VMRS.

Code Key 35-40 and 47-48 describe major component configurations. Similarly, Code Keys 53-75 provide the means to record similar data for mechanical refrigeration and material handling equipment.

Code Key 79 offers position codes for components which may be used in more than one location, orientation or position. Code Key 80 identifies severity of service for various types of vehicle applications/vocations. Code Key 81 identifies types of claims for warranty processing. Code Key 82 describes driver/ operator vehicle complaints for warranty and driver condition report processing. Code Keys 83 and 84 pertain to warranty claim status and response.

VMRS "Instruction Sets" are composite codes - derived from combinations of various Code Keys - that serve as "equipment type codes" for power units, trailers, and converters. These Instruction Sets are numerical sentences, using individual Code Keys as building blocks or "words" to describe various aspects of equipment specification or labor activity. There are 15 VMRS Instruction Sets currently in use. (VMRS Instruction Sets were previously classified as Code Keys. Beginning with VMRS 2000 v.1.01, the term Instruction Set is used instead for these "composite" identifiers.)

This section offers a complete list of all VMRS Instruction Sets, Code Keys and their corresponding values. Together, they represent the most powerful coding convention available for classifying and identifying all aspects of equipment maintenance and maintenance management.

If you—the user—find deficiencies in these Code Keys, please call TMC. TMC staff will be happy to either locate existing codes or assign new codes for your operation. Only you—the end-user—can help VMRS remain a dynamic standard.

All inquiries regarding VMRS Code Keys should be directed to:

Technology & Maintenance Council American Trucking Associations 950 N. Glebe Road, Suite 210 Arlington, VA 22203 (703) 838-1763. Email: tmc@trucking.org

# **Code Key 1: Equipment Vocation**

#### Description and Purpose

Code Key 1 is an adjective description of the primary industry area of a unit's operation. Put otherwise, Code Key 1 describes what a unit *does*. For Codes 10-90—which were originally created for the motor carrier industry—the first digit of the code corresponds to the activities defined in the Uniform System of Accounts. (The Uniform System of Accounts was originally developed by the Interstate Commerce Commission.) All other codes assigned to Code Key 1 do not follow this convention. The second digit further subdivides activity for more definitive identification.

#### Use

Code Key 1 is used in all VMRS Equipment Master Record Forms. On *"Form 1,* Equipment Master Record—Power Units," it is entered in the field identified as "Equip. Voc" (6).

# **Code Key 3: Axle Configuration**

#### Description and Purpose

Code Key 3 describes axle configurations for all types of equipment, trailers and converter dollies. Where used, the first number in the description indicates the total number of wheels, and the second indicates the number of driven wheels. Therefore, a 4x2 piece of equipment has four wheels, with one powered axle with two driven wheels; or a 6x4 piece of equipment has three axles with six wheels, with two powered axles with four driven wheels. Wheels are considered a unit, whether they have single or dual tires.

Use

Code Key 3 is used with VMRS Equipment Master Record Forms. On *"Form 1,* Equipment Master Record—Power Units," it is entered as the second character of the Equipment Type Code, Line A5, see instruction set 5. On *"Form 2,* Equipment Master Record—Trailers, Containers and Converters," it is entered as the second character of the Equipment Type Code, Line A5 as well.

# Code Key 4: Cab Types (All Equipment)

#### Description and Purpose

Code Key 4 describes cab types for all types of equipment, including material handling equipment. A cab is considered to be a compartment used by an individual to operate a piece of equipment.

#### Use

Code Key 4 is used with VMRS Equipment Master Record Forms. On *"Form 1,* Equipment Master Record—Power Units," it is entered as the third character of the Equipment Type Code, Line A5, see Instruction 5. On Form 4, it is entered on Line A5 as well.

# Code Key 7: Transmission Types For Power Units

#### Description and Purpose

Code Key 7 identifies transmission types for power units.

#### Use

Code Key 7 is used with VMRS Equipment Master Record forms. On *"Form 1,* Equipment Master Record—Power Units," it is entered in the Equipment Type Code, Line A5, see Instruction Set 5 and Transmission Type Codes, Lines H7 and J5, respectively. See Instruction Set 2

**NOTE:** *Semi-automatic transmissions* allow the driver to select and retain control of the desired ratio. Shifting is accomplished electrically, hydraulically or pneumatically without driver synchronization. *Automated transmissions* feature sophisticated computer management of shifting functions and/or "shift by wire" technology. With automated transmissions, the clutch is used for starting and stopping only.

| Code | Transmission Type                                                                         |
|------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1    | Manual                                                                                    |
| 2    | Automatic                                                                                 |
| 3    | Semi-Automatic (driver selects and controls desired ratio, does not synchronize shifting) |
| 4    | Automated                                                                                 |
| 9    | Does Not Apply                                                                            |

# Code Key 14: Reason for Repair

### Description and Purpose

Code Key 14 describes the reasons why work was performed on a unit. These codes fall into one of three specific categories:

- Maintenance or repairs directly attributable to a piece of equipment. This is work performed to maintain or restore equipment to a specified operating condition, which is directly attributable to its operation. This includes inspecting, repairing, or replacing any defective part or assembly which requires attention.
- Work performed based on management decision. Work which is not directly attributable equipment operation, such as a change to its original configuration, or rehabilitation to the extent that the costs incurred are capitalized. Also includes the special review, or inspection, of equipment so that information can be obtained for management decision purposes.
- Repairs caused by outside influence. This is worked performed which is not directly attributable equipment operation or based upon a management decision. Often many of the costs incurred in this category are subsequently reimbursed in whole or in part by an outside source.

#### Use

Code Key 14 is used when completing VMRS Repair Order forms (*Form 6*) and VMRS Special Repair Order forms (*Form 7*). Selecting the appropriate reason for repair is very important as it impacts management decisions made based on this information.
